formatted_review:
The proposed Phase III clinical trial for tanezumab is designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the drug in treating moderate to severe osteoarthritis of the knee through an open-label, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial structure. The trial will involve two treatment arms: one receiving tanezumab at a dosage of 5 mg/kg every four weeks, and a placebo group, with a total sample size of 1,000 participants. Randomization will be stratified by age, sex, and disease severity, ensuring a balanced representation across these variables. The trial duration is set for two years, with a 12-month follow-up period post-treatment, providing a comprehensive timeframe to assess both immediate and long-term effects of the treatment.

In terms of inclusion and exclusion criteria, the trial appropriately targets patients with moderate to severe osteoarthritis of the knee, while excluding those with previous joint replacement surgeries or those on conflicting medications, to minimize confounding variables and safety risks. The primary objectives focus on evaluating tanezumab's effectiveness in pain reduction, functional improvement, and its impact on quality of life and patient-reported outcomes. These objectives align well with the current clinical priorities in osteoarthritis management and the existing unmet needs in this patient population.

The risk assessment of the trial identifies a moderate overall risk level with certain domains requiring targeted mitigation strategies. The mechanistic risk is low, given the well-characterized mechanism of tanezumab targeting RANKL. However, to enhance understanding of off-target effects that could lead to adverse events, a supplementary mechanistic study is recommended. Alternatively, a meta-analysis of existing data from terminated trials could provide insights into the drug's broader impact.

Biomarker risk is classified as medium due to the ongoing validation of secondary and exploratory biomarkers. To address this, the incorporation of exploratory biomarkers focusing on inflammation and joint degeneration is suggested. This strategy is supported by evidence in rheumatology where such biomarkers have improved understanding of disease progression and treatment response. If development of new biomarkers is challenging, established imaging techniques like MRI should be utilized as surrogate biomarkers.

The endpoint risk also falls into the medium category, with a strong recommendation to include patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) alongside traditional clinical endpoints. PROMs have shown to provide valuable insights into patient quality of life and treatment satisfaction, integral to assessing overall treatment efficacy. Should integrating PROMs present difficulties, leveraging digital health tools for real-time symptom monitoring is an advisable alternative.

Safety risk management is crucial due to known adverse events associated with tanezumab, such as hypersensitivity reactions, infection risks, and potential bone health concerns. A robust adverse event monitoring system is recommended, with a focus on early detection of osteonecrosis and cardiovascular issues through clinical assessments and imaging techniques. If comprehensive monitoring proves infeasible, a dose adjustment strategy could be employed, beginning with lower doses and adjusting based on patient tolerance and safety outcomes.

In conclusion, the proposed trial for tanezumab in the treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee is well-structured, with a clear focus on addressing key clinical endpoints while implementing a comprehensive risk mitigation strategy. By integrating mechanistic studies, exploratory biomarkers, patient-reported outcomes, and robust safety monitoring, the trial aims to provide valuable insights into the drug's efficacy and safety profile. These measures will not only enhance the trial's scientific rigor but also ensure patient safety and data integrity, aligning well with FDA regulatory standards and expectations.

14.4 Ankylosing Spondylitis
The efficacy and safety were assessed in 332 patients in one randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study [Trial AS-1 (NCT03928743)] in adult subjects 18 years of age and older with active ankylosing spondylitis. Subjects had to have documented radiologic evidence (x-ray) fulfilling the Modified New York criteria for AS. Subjects had active disease as defined by BASDAI ≥4 and spinal pain ≥4 on a 0 to 10 numeric rating scale (NRS) (from BASDAI Item 2). Subjects also had a history of inadequate response to 2 different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or intolerance or contraindication to NSAIDs. Approximately 20% of subjects were on concomitant cDMARDs. Overall, 16% of subjects had received previous treatment (failed or were intolerant to) with anti-TNF alpha agents.
Subjects were randomized 2:1 to receive BIMZELX 160 mg or placebo every 4 weeks up to the completion of Week 16 assessments. Starting at Week 16, all subjects received BIMZELX every 4 weeks up to Week 52. The primary endpoint was at least 40% improvement in Assessment of Spondyloarthritis International Society (ASAS 40) at Week 16.
Clinical Response
In Trial AS-1, treatment with BIMZELX resulted in significant improvements in the measure of disease activity compared to placebo at Week 16 (Table 9).

14.3 Psoriatic Arthritis
The safety and efficacy of ustekinumab was assessed in 927 subjects (PsA STUDY 1, n=615; PsA STUDY 2, n=312), in two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in adult subjects 18 years of age and older with active PsA (≥5 swollen joints and ≥5 tender joints) despite non- steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) or disease modifying antirheumatic (DMARD) therapy. Subjects in these trials had a diagnosis of PsA for at least 6 months. Subjects with each subtype of PsA were enrolled, including polyarticular arthritis with the absence of rheumatoid nodules (39%), spondylitis with peripheral arthritis (28%), asymmetric peripheral arthritis (21%), distal interphalangeal involvement (12%) and arthritis mutilans (0.5%). Over 70% and 40% of the subjects, respectively, had enthesitis and dactylitis at baseline.

Patients in the active groups may have crossed over to the alternate active dose group, and results are reported per original randomized dose group.
In the placebo group, 66% of patients experienced no radiographic progression (Total Sharp-Genant Score change ≤ 0) at week 52 compared to 78% and 83% in the tocilizumab 4 mg per kg and 8 mg per kg, respectively. Following 104 weeks of treatment, 75% and 83% of patients initially randomized to tocilizumab 4 mg per kg and 8 mg per kg, respectively, experienced no progression of structural damage compared to 66% of placebo treated patients.
Health Related Outcomes
In Study II, physical function and disability were assessed using the Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index (HAQ-DI). Both dosing groups of tocilizumab demonstrated a greater improvement compared to the placebo group in the AUC of change from baseline in the HAQ-DI through week 52. The mean change from baseline to week 52 in HAQ-DI was 0.6, 0.5, and 0.4 for tocilizumab 8 mg per kg, tocilizumab 4 mg per kg, and placebo treatment groups, respectively. Sixty-three percent (63%) and sixty percent (60%) of patients in the tocilizumab 8 mg per kg and tocilizumab 4 mg per kg treatment groups, respectively, achieved a clinically relevant improvement in HAQ-DI (change from baseline of ≥ 0.3 units) at week 52 compared to 53% in the placebo treatment group.
Other Health-Related Outcomes
General health status was assessed by the Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) in Studies I – V. Patients receiving tocilizumab demonstrated greater improvement from baseline compared to placebo in the Physical Component Summary (PCS), Mental Component Summary (MCS), and in all 8 domains of the SF-36.
